lessons.title: Introduction to Taxonomy and Classification: Why Do Our Groupings Differ?

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kericho, a fisher at Lake Victoria and a student in Nairobi each sort the same eight organisms: goat, chicken, maize plant, mushroom, algae, bacteria, bean plant and mosquito. Which prediction is most reasonable?
choices: Only the student in Nairobi can make correct groups
They may make different groups, because each person may choose a different rule such as habitat, use or size
They must make the same groups, because the organisms are the same
They cannot make any groups, because the organisms are too different
quiz.rationale: People can sort using different rules (habitat, food use, colour, movement), so different groupings are possible. Predictions are not marked wrong at this stage, but this one fits the idea of different criteria.
quiz.placement: Predict: individual written prediction and Think-Pair-Share on whether the farmer, fisher and student will make the same groups

quiz.prompt: A group sorts the organisms with the rule: 'Can move from place to place on its own.' Which set contains only organisms that clearly fit this rule?
choices: Goat, maize plant, mushroom
Mushroom, algae, bean plant
Goat, chicken, mosquito
Chicken, bean plant, mosquito
quiz.rationale: A goat, a chicken and a mosquito all clearly move from place to place on their own. Maize, bean plants and mushrooms stay fixed in one place.
quiz.placement: Observe: card sorting, Step 1, where the group agrees one rule and sorts the eight cards

quiz.prompt: In a card-sorting activity, Group A put the mushroom with the plants and Group C put the mushroom in a different group. Both groups wrote a clear rule. What does this show?
choices: The mushroom cannot be classified at all
The same organism can be placed in different groups when groups use different rules
Group C cheated, because the mushroom can only go with plants
Both groups must have misread the cards
quiz.rationale: Each group used its own criterion, so the same organism ended up in different groups. This was the key observation from the Gallery Walk.
quiz.placement: Observe: Gallery Walk, finding an organism placed in a different group from your own

quiz.prompt: Maize is called 'mahindi' in Kiswahili, and it has different names in Kikuyu, Luo and English. What problem can this cause?
choices: People using different names may not be sure they are talking about the same organism
Only the Kiswahili name is allowed in science
Names do not matter because everyone already uses the same groups
Maize will grow differently in each community
quiz.rationale: Different local names for one organism make it hard for people in different places to be sure they mean the same living thing.
quiz.placement: Observe: Step 4, listing Kikuyu, Luo, Kiswahili and English names for the same organism in a table

quiz.prompt: One group sorted the eight organisms by usefulness: food, pests and disease-causing. Another learner says, 'That group is wrong.' Which response fits what the class found?
choices: The group is wrong, because organisms cannot be both useful and harmful
The learner is right, because only habitat can be used to sort organisms
The group is not wrong, because it followed a clear rule, but its rule is only one of many possible rules
The learner is right, because usefulness is not a real feature
quiz.rationale: Every group was correct by its own criterion. The puzzle is that many correct groupings exist, so no single one works for everyone.
quiz.placement: Explain: debate on 'Is the group that sorted by usefulness (food, pests, disease) wrong?'

quiz.prompt: Which statement best describes what 'classification' means, as used in this lesson?
choices: Finding the most useful organism
Grouping organisms using chosen criteria (rules)
Collecting organisms from the environment
Giving every organism a new name
quiz.rationale: In this lesson, classification means grouping organisms using chosen criteria. Different criteria give different groupings.
quiz.placement: Explain: Jigsaw/peer teaching question 'What is classification?'

quiz.prompt: At the end of Lesson 1, learners draw an initial model with a 'what we need' box. Which idea best fits what a shared system for classifying organisms should provide?
choices: Only people in Nairobi decide the groups
Only organisms that are useful for food are included
Each community keeps its own names and rules, and nobody changes them
The same names and rules that people everywhere can use to identify and study organisms
quiz.rationale: The puzzle was that different groupings and names stop people communicating, so a shared system needs common names and rules usable by everyone. The lesson does not yet say what that system is.
quiz.placement: Model: drawing the initial model with the 'problem' arrow and the 'what we need' box

lessons.title: Importance of Classification: Why Do We Need to Identify Organisms Correctly?

quiz.prompt: A family in Kakamega collects wild mushrooms for supper. They call an edible mushroom and a poisonous look-alike by the same local name. What is the most likely problem?
choices: They will only lose money because the mushrooms cannot be sold
Nothing, because two organisms with the same name must be the same species
Both mushrooms will become safe to eat once they are cooked
They may cook and eat a poisonous mushroom, believing it is safe
quiz.rationale: If two different mushrooms share one name, people cannot tell which is edible, so someone may eat the poisonous one and get food poisoning. A shared name does not make organisms the same.
quiz.placement: Predict: Think-Pair-Share on 'What could go wrong if people in Kisumu, Nairobi and Kericho identify these organisms differently?'

quiz.prompt: Learners studied edible and poisonous mushrooms using photographs only. Which approach helps tell an edible mushroom from a deadly look-alike?
choices: Assume all mushrooms growing in the wild are safe
Taste a small piece and see if it makes you sick
Choose the mushroom with the name your family has always used
Compare features such as the cap, gills, ring and base
quiz.rationale: Identification depends on observing features such as the cap, gills, ring and base. Tasting and assuming all mushrooms are safe are dangerous, and a local name alone may refer to several kinds.
quiz.placement: Observe: Case A, edible versus poisonous mushrooms (features such as cap, gills, ring, base)

quiz.prompt: Which statement about insects is correct, based on the honey bee, ladybird, mosquito and locust?
choices: An insect is harmful only if it is large
All insects are pests and should be killed
All insects are useful, so none need to be controlled
Some insects are useful, such as honey bees and ladybirds, while others harm people or crops, such as mosquitoes and locusts
quiz.rationale: Honey bees pollinate and make honey, and ladybirds help control pests. Mosquitoes spread malaria and locusts destroy crops. Correct identification tells us which insects to protect and which to control.
quiz.placement: Observe: Case B, useful versus harmful insects (honey bee and ladybird against mosquito, locust and tsetse fly)

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kericho must tell maize from couch grass and beans from black jack (Bidens pilosa) before weeding or spraying. Why does this identification matter?
choices: Weeds are plants, so they never affect the crop
Black jack and couch grass are useful crops and should be protected
Weeds make the crop taste bitter but do not affect its growth
Weeds compete with crops for light, water and nutrients, and spraying the wrong plant could kill the crop
quiz.rationale: Weeds compete with crops for light, water and nutrients. A farmer who cannot identify crop and weed correctly may spray or remove the wrong plant and lose the harvest.
quiz.placement: Observe: Case C, crops versus weeds (maize and beans against couch grass and black jack; herbicide choice)

quiz.prompt: Why are local names (in Kikuyu, Luo, Kiswahili or English) alone not enough for scientists to communicate about organisms across Kenya and the world?
choices: The same organism can have different names in different languages, so people may not be sure they mean the same organism
Local names are always wrong and local knowledge should be ignored
Local names are too short to describe an organism
Only English names can be used to describe living things
quiz.rationale: Local names are valuable, but one organism may have many names and different organisms may share one name. A common system is needed so everyone is sure which organism is meant.
quiz.placement: Explain: Discussion and debate 'Is local knowledge enough, or do we also need a universal system?'

quiz.prompt: A group writes the claim 'Classification is important because it helps us identify organisms safely.' Which statement is the best piece of EVIDENCE to support this claim?
choices: Maize is grown in many parts of Kenya
Classification is very useful to scientists
A poisonous mushroom can look like an edible oyster mushroom, so wrongly identifying it can cause poisoning
Many Kenyans enjoy eating mushrooms
quiz.rationale: Evidence is a specific fact or case that supports the claim. The poisonous look-alike mushroom shows what can happen when organisms are not identified correctly. The other options are claims or unrelated facts.
quiz.placement: Explain: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) statement 'Why is classification important?'

quiz.prompt: Learners agreed that everyone was correct by their own criteria (habitat, colour, usefulness) and that classification helps us identify, study and communicate about organisms. What is still MISSING from the class model?
choices: More local names for each organism
A common system of groups that everyone agrees to use
More ways to sort organisms by colour and size
More photographs of poisonous mushrooms
quiz.rationale: Different personal criteria and local names cause confusion. The model still needs a shared set of groups that all scientists use, which becomes the next question for the class.
quiz.placement: Model: revising the class model and adding the 'What is still missing?' box

lessons.title: Taxonomic Units: From Kingdom to Species

quiz.prompt: A Kenyan address goes from the biggest area to the smallest area. Scientists place organisms in groups inside groups in a similar way. Which list of address levels is in the correct order from biggest to smallest?
choices: County, Country, Ward, Sub-county, Village
Country, County, Sub-county, Ward, Village
Village, Ward, Sub-county, County, Country
Country, Village, Ward, Sub-county, County
quiz.rationale: A country contains counties, which contain sub-counties, then wards, then villages. The address is a nested system, just like taxonomic ranks, which go from the biggest group to the smallest.
quiz.placement: Predict: Kenyan address analogy and Think-Pair-Share

quiz.prompt: Which list shows the seven taxonomic ranks in the correct order from the broadest group to the most specific group?
choices: Kingdom, Phylum/Division, Class, Family, Order, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Class, Phylum/Division, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum/Division, Kingdom
Kingdom, Phylum/Division, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
quiz.rationale: The correct order from broadest to most specific is Kingdom, Phylum/Division, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. One distractor reverses Order and Family, one swaps Phylum and Class, and one lists the ranks from most specific to broadest.
quiz.placement: Card sorting investigation, Step 1: arrange the rank cards from broadest to most specific

quiz.prompt: As you move down the ranks from Kingdom to Species, what happens to the number of organisms in each group and to the features they share?
choices: There are fewer organisms in each group and they share fewer features
The number of organisms and the shared features stay the same
There are fewer organisms in each group and they share more features
There are more organisms in each group and they share more features
quiz.rationale: Each rank is nested inside the one above it, so groups get smaller. Organisms in a smaller group are more alike, so they share more features. The funnel diagram in the activity shows this.
quiz.placement: Card sorting investigation, Step 3: 'funnel' diagram counting organisms at each rank

quiz.prompt: Maize is classified in this order from broadest to most specific: Plantae, Angiospermophyta, Monocotyledonae, Poales, Poaceae, Zea, Zea mays. Which taxonomic rank is Poaceae?
choices: Genus
Family
Class
Order
quiz.rationale: The ranks run Kingdom (Plantae), Division (Angiospermophyta), Class (Monocotyledonae), Order (Poales), Family (Poaceae), Genus (Zea), Species (Zea mays). Poaceae is the fifth group, so it is the Family.
quiz.placement: Card sorting investigation, Step 2: match organism-category cards to each rank for the maize plant

quiz.prompt: A Kikuyu speaker, a Luo speaker and a Kiswahili speaker each use a different local name for the same animal. Why does the nested ranking system (Kingdom to Species) help them?
choices: It gives every organism one exact place in the system, so all of them can find the same organism whatever its local name
It replaces all local names so that people stop using them
It puts all animals with similar local names into the same group
It sorts organisms by where they live, so everyone agrees on the habitat
quiz.rationale: Nesting gives each organism one unique position from Kingdom to Species, so people who use different local names can still identify the same organism. The system does not sort by habitat and does not need local names to be abandoned.
quiz.placement: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning: How are the taxonomic ranks related from the largest group to the smallest?

quiz.prompt: Animals are placed in a Phylum. What is the name of the rank at the same level, directly below Kingdom, that is used for plants such as maize?
choices: Class
Genus
Division
Family
quiz.rationale: The second rank is called Phylum for animals and Division for plants. Class, Family and Genus are lower ranks and are not the plant version of Phylum.
quiz.placement: Class discussion after Claim-Evidence-Reasoning: clarifying Phylum and Division

quiz.prompt: The lion is classified as Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Carnivora, Felidae, Panthera, Panthera leo. Maize is classified as Plantae, Angiospermophyta, Monocotyledonae, Poales, Poaceae, Zea, Zea mays. Comparing the two lists rank by rank, in how many of the seven ranks do the lion and maize belong to the same group?
choices: 2 ranks
7 ranks
1 rank
0 ranks
quiz.rationale: The lion and maize already differ at Kingdom (Animalia and Plantae). Because each rank is nested inside the one above, they are in different groups at every rank below it too, so they share no group at any of the seven ranks.
quiz.placement: Model revision: adding the 'nested ladder' section with the lion (Panthera leo) and maize (Zea mays) examples

lessons.title: Hierarchy of Classification: Climbing the Taxonomic Staircase

quiz.prompt: Which list shows the seven main taxonomic levels in the correct order, from the broadest group to the most specific group?
choices: Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom
Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Genus, Family, Species
Kingdom, Class, Phylum, Order, Family, Genus, Species
quiz.rationale: The hierarchy runs Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species, from the broadest group to the most specific. The other lists swap levels or run in reverse.
quiz.placement: Part A: Video 2 note-catcher on the order of the seven levels

quiz.prompt: A learner moves down the taxonomic staircase from Family to Genus. What happens to the group of organisms?
choices: The group has fewer kinds of organisms, and they are more alike
The group has more kinds of organisms, and they are less alike
The group has fewer kinds of organisms, but they are less alike
The group has the same number of organisms, but they are named differently
quiz.rationale: Each step down the hierarchy is nested inside the one above. So it holds fewer kinds of organisms that share more features.
quiz.placement: Part B: taxonomic staircase card sorting (how groups change going down the hierarchy)

quiz.prompt: A goat is classified as Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia. A domestic chicken is classified as Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Aves. At which level do the goat and the chicken first separate into different groups?
choices: Species
Class
Phylum
Kingdom
quiz.rationale: The goat and chicken share Kingdom Animalia and Phylum Chordata. They first differ at Class, where the goat is Mammalia and the chicken is Aves.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw: mixed groups compare the goat and chicken staircases

quiz.prompt: In the classification of a goat (Capra hircus), the name Bovidae is given. At which taxonomic level does the name Bovidae belong?
choices: Family
Order
Class
Genus
quiz.rationale: For the goat, Artiodactyla is the Order and Bovidae is the Family. Capra is the Genus and Capra hircus is the Species.
quiz.placement: Part B: filling in each level of the assigned organism (goat example) using the chart

quiz.prompt: Which statement about the Species level is correct?
choices: Species is the second level, coming straight after Kingdom
Species and Genus are the same level, so they mean the same thing
Species is the biggest group, because it contains all the other levels
Species is the most specific level, with the smallest group of the most similar organisms
quiz.rationale: Species is the last and narrowest step of the staircase. It holds the smallest group of organisms that are most alike, and Genus is a separate, broader level above it.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw and CER: addressing misconceptions such as 'Species is the biggest group'

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kericho and a student in Kisumu both use the taxonomic staircase from Kingdom to Species to classify a goat. Which problem is solved, and which problem still remains?
choices: Solved: all local names in Kikuyu, Luo and Kiswahili are now the same. Remaining: goats cannot be placed in a Kingdom.
Solved: both can place the goat in the same position at every level. Remaining: we still need one unique name for each species that is recognised worldwide.
Solved: every organism now has one unique worldwide name. Remaining: people cannot agree on the order of the seven levels.
Solved: organisms are grouped by colour and size in the same way everywhere. Remaining: nothing, because the system is complete.
quiz.rationale: The ranked hierarchy lets everyone put the goat in the same place at each level. The staircase does not yet give each species one agreed name, which leads to the next lesson.
quiz.placement: Model revision: marking the gap 'We still need one unique name for each species'

lessons.title: Scientific Names and Binomial Nomenclature: One Name for Every Organism

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kisumu and a researcher in Nairobi each use only their own local name for a mosquito species when sharing information about malaria control. What problem is most likely to happen?
choices: Local names are always wrong, so neither person can describe the mosquito
The mosquito will change its behaviour depending on the name used
They may not be sure they are talking about the same organism, so mistakes can happen
The mosquito can only be studied by people who speak Kiswahili
quiz.rationale: Common names vary by place and language, so two people may use different names for the same organism, or the same name for different ones. This causes confusion in farming, medicine and pest control.
quiz.placement: Predict: individual prediction and Think-Pair-Share on problems that arise when people use only their own local names

quiz.prompt: In some countries the word 'corn' means maize, but in other countries it means a different cereal. What does this show about common names?
choices: A common name always tells us exactly which species an organism is
Common names are only used for plants, never for animals
Common names are the same everywhere in the world
The same common name can refer to different organisms, which causes confusion
quiz.rationale: One common name can refer to different organisms in different places. This is one reason a universal name is needed.
quiz.placement: Part A: Name Comparison Table, examples where one common name refers to different organisms

quiz.prompt: You want to handwrite the scientific name of the goat, Capra hircus, following the rules of binomial nomenclature. What should you do?
choices: Underline the genus and the species separately
Write the whole name in capital letters instead of underlining
Underline the whole name with one continuous line so the two words are joined
Write the name in brackets so that it can be told apart from other words
quiz.rationale: Scientific names are written in italics when typed. When handwritten, the genus and the species are each underlined separately.
quiz.placement: Part C: Jigsaw, expert rule 3 (italics or underlining each part separately)

quiz.prompt: A learner writes the scientific name of the mosquito as Anopheles Gambiae. Which rule of binomial nomenclature has been broken?
choices: The species name must start with a small letter
The genus must start with a small letter
A scientific name must be written in Kiswahili
A scientific name must have three parts
quiz.rationale: The genus begins with a capital letter and the species begins with a small letter. The correct form is Anopheles gambiae.
quiz.placement: Card-sorting task: sorting 'Correct' and 'Incorrect' name cards and explaining which rule was broken

quiz.prompt: A group writes the claim: 'Scientists need a scientific name for each organism even though people already have common names.' Which reasoning best supports this claim?
choices: Scientific names are longer than common names, so they are more useful
Scientific names are in Latin, and Latin is the easiest language for everyone to speak
Local names are wrong and should not be used by anyone
Each organism has one accepted two-part name used worldwide, so scientists everywhere know which organism is meant and can share information without confusion
quiz.rationale: Good reasoning links the evidence (common names differ, but Zea mays is the same everywhere) to the idea that a universal name avoids confusion.
quiz.placement: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) explanation: 'Why do scientists need a scientific name for each organism?'

quiz.prompt: In a class debate, a learner says: 'Now that we have scientific names, we should stop using local names like mbuzi, mbũri and diel.' Which response is best?
choices: Disagree, because local names remain valuable in communities, while scientific names are used for communication among scientists worldwide
Agree, because scientific names replace local names completely
Disagree, because scientific names can only be used for plants
Agree, because local names are never correct
quiz.rationale: Scientific names do not replace local names. Local names keep their cultural and community value, and scientific names give one shared name for universal scientific communication.
quiz.placement: Class discussion and debate: 'Should we stop using local names now that we have scientific names?'

quiz.prompt: Learners add a Naming Layer to the class model and label the scientific name of the goat, Capra hircus. Which labelling is correct?
choices: Genus: Capra hircus; Species: goat
Genus: mbuzi; Species: Capra hircus
Genus: hircus; Species: Capra
Genus: Capra; Species: hircus
quiz.rationale: The first word, written with a capital letter, is the genus (Capra). The second word, written with a small letter, is the species (hircus).
quiz.placement: Revising the class classification model: Naming Layer diagram labelling genus and species

lessons.title: Applying Binomial Nomenclature: Naming Our Local Organisms the Same Way Everywhere

quiz.prompt: In Kenya, maize is called 'mahindi' in Kiswahili, 'mbembe' in Kikuyu and 'oganda' in Luo. Why is this a problem for scientists who share information with scientists in other countries?
choices: Only English names can be used for plants
Local names are wrong and must never be used
Different languages use different names, so people may not know they are talking about the same organism
Maize has too many parts to be named
quiz.rationale: The same organism has many local names, so a name in one language may not be understood elsewhere. A universal name is needed. Local names are not wrong; they are just not shared by everyone.
quiz.placement: Predict: organism cards and the prediction 'what name could they both use so nobody is confused?'

quiz.prompt: A learner types the scientific name of maize. Which way follows the rules for writing a scientific name (ignoring italics)?
choices: Zea mays
Zea Mays
zea mays
zea Mays
quiz.rationale: A scientific name has two parts. The genus starts with a capital letter and the species starts with a small letter, so it is written 'Zea mays'.
quiz.placement: Observe: Jigsaw, rule (2) genus starts with a capital, species with a small letter

quiz.prompt: You are writing the scientific name of the goat, Capra hircus, by hand in your exercise book. How should you show that it is a scientific name?
choices: Draw one long line under both words together
Underline Capra and hircus separately, each with its own line
Put the name in brackets and do not underline
Write both words in capital letters
quiz.rationale: Typed names are in italics. When handwritten, the genus and the species are each underlined separately.
quiz.placement: Observe: Jigsaw, rule (3) italics when printed, underline each part separately when handwritten

quiz.prompt: A group is matching scientific names to organism cards. Which organism is correctly matched with the scientific name Phaseolus vulgaris?
choices: Bean plant
Mosquito
Goat
Maize
quiz.rationale: Phaseolus vulgaris is the scientific name of the bean plant. Zea mays is maize, Capra hircus is the goat and Anopheles gambiae is the mosquito.
quiz.placement: Observe: group table matching scientific names to the organism cards

quiz.prompt: A learner writes the scientific name of the goat as 'Capra Hircus'. What is wrong with it?
choices: Both words should start with a small letter
The genus should start with a small letter
The species 'Hircus' should start with a small letter
Scientific names should be written in English
quiz.rationale: Only the genus begins with a capital letter. The species starts with a small letter, so the correct name is 'Capra hircus'. This is a common error of capitalising the species.
quiz.placement: Explain: worksheet 'Fix the Names'

quiz.prompt: A learner writes a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning answer claiming that Zea mays is a better name for scientists than mahindi, mbembe or oganda. Which reasoning best supports the claim?
choices: The same two-part name is used worldwide, so everyone can identify the same organism
Zea mays is shorter and easier to say than the local names
Local names are incorrect and should not be used
Zea mays is older than all the local names
quiz.rationale: A scientific name is the same everywhere, so scientists in any country know which organism is meant. Local names differ by language, but they are not wrong.
quiz.placement: Explain: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning response on why Zea mays is a better name

quiz.prompt: In a class debate, a learner says: 'Local names are not important when we have scientific names.' Which response is best?
choices: Agree, because local names are always wrong
Disagree, because local names are never used in science
Agree, because scientific names replace local names
Disagree, because local names such as mbembe and oganda have cultural and practical value, while scientific names allow worldwide communication
quiz.rationale: Scientific names do not replace local names. Local names carry cultural and practical value in communities, and scientific names let people everywhere communicate about the same organism.
quiz.placement: Explain: discussion and debate on 'Local names are not important when we have scientific names'

quiz.prompt: Groups once sorted a goat, chicken, maize, mushroom, algae, bacteria, bean plant and mosquito by colour, habitat and usefulness, and every group was right by its own rules. Which basis for grouping can be checked by anyone, in any country, and give the same result?
choices: The colour and size of the organism
How useful or harmful the organism is to people
Cell type and how the organism gets its food
What the organism is called in Kikuyu, Luo or Kiswahili
quiz.rationale: Cell type and mode of nutrition are structural and feeding characteristics that can be checked by anyone. Colour, size, usefulness and local names change from person to person or place to place.
quiz.placement: Predict: Think-Pair-Share on how scientists would group the eight organisms

quiz.prompt: Learners studying bacteria and the fermented milk maziwa lala record the cell type on their Kingdom Data Card. Which kingdom is made of prokaryotic cells?
choices: Plantae
Monera
Protoctista
Fungi
quiz.rationale: Monera (bacteria and cyanobacteria) is the only kingdom of prokaryotic cells with no true nucleus. Protoctista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia are all eukaryotic.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw Step 1: expert groups completing the Kingdom Data Card (Monera evidence pack)

quiz.prompt: A learner looks at green Spirogyra from a pond jar and says, 'It is green and lives in water, so it is a plant.' Which is the best response?
choices: Correct, all green organisms belong to Kingdom Plantae
Wrong, Spirogyra is an animal because it lives in water
Wrong, Spirogyra and other algae belong to Kingdom Protoctista, so being green does not make an organism a plant
Wrong, Spirogyra is a fungus because it grows in water
quiz.rationale: Algae such as Spirogyra are placed in Protoctista. Kingdoms are decided by shared characteristics such as cell type, organisation and nutrition, not by colour or habitat.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw Step 1: Protoctista expert group (Spirogyra or green pond water, algae from Lake Victoria)

quiz.prompt: A mushroom grows from the soil next to a maize plant. Why is the mushroom NOT placed in Kingdom Plantae?
choices: It is a prokaryote, so it cannot be a plant
It is not green, so it must be an animal
It cannot make its own food (it is heterotrophic) and its cell wall is made of chitin
It grows in soil, which only fungi do
quiz.rationale: A mushroom is a fungus. It feeds on organic matter instead of making food by photosynthesis, and its cell wall contains chitin. Growing in soil does not make an organism a plant.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw Step 2: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning debate on the mushroom

quiz.prompt: A learner writes a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning statement placing the mosquito in Kingdom Animalia. Which reasoning is the strongest?
choices: It is a pest that spreads disease
It is a multicellular eukaryote that feeds on other organisms (heterotrophic)
It lives near water and is active at night
It is small and has wings, like a chicken
quiz.rationale: Animalia is defined by cell type, organisation and nutrition: multicellular, eukaryotic and heterotrophic. Being a pest, having wings or living near water are appearance, habitat or usefulness ideas, not kingdom characteristics.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw Step 2: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning and card sort of the eight organisms

quiz.prompt: A group revises its class model and places the eight organisms into kingdoms. Which placement is correct?
choices: Bacteria in Monera, algae in Protoctista and mushroom in Fungi
Bacteria in Protoctista and goat in Animalia
Algae in Plantae and mushroom in Fungi
Mushroom in Plantae and bacteria in Monera
quiz.rationale: Bacteria are prokaryotes (Monera), algae are in Protoctista, and the mushroom is a fungus. Placing algae or the mushroom in Plantae, or bacteria in Protoctista, is a common error.
quiz.placement: Model: groups revise the class classification model with the eight phenomenon organisms placed in kingdoms

quiz.prompt: Which list names the five taxonomic kingdoms of living organisms?
choices: Monera, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia, Viruses
Monera, Protoctista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia
Plantae, Animalia, Fungi, Bacteria, Insects
Bacteria, Algae, Mushrooms, Plants, Mammals
quiz.rationale: The five kingdoms are Monera, Protoctista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. The other lists include groups such as algae, mammals, insects or viruses that are not kingdoms in this system.
quiz.placement: End of lesson: summary of the five-kingdom system

lessons.title: Classification into the Five Kingdoms and Importance of Taxonomy: Our Final Explanation

quiz.prompt: A single-celled organism from a pond has a nucleus, moves using temporary extensions of its body (pseudopodia) and takes in food particles. Which kingdom does it belong to?
choices: Fungi
Plantae
Monera
Protoctista
quiz.rationale: A unicellular organism with a nucleus is eukaryotic, so it cannot be in Monera (prokaryotes). Amoeba-type organisms belong to Kingdom Protoctista.
quiz.placement: Expert groups: evidence table for Group A (Monera and Protoctista: Amoeba, Spirogyra, Paramecium)

quiz.prompt: A mushroom grows in soil. It has no chlorophyll and absorbs food from decaying matter. Which kingdom does it belong to, and why?
choices: Animalia, because it cannot make its own food
Plantae, because it grows in soil
Fungi, because it has no chlorophyll and absorbs nutrients from its surroundings
Protoctista, because it has no leaves or roots
quiz.rationale: Fungi are eukaryotic, non-photosynthetic and absorb food from their surroundings. Growing in soil does not make an organism a plant.
quiz.placement: Group B (Fungi: Rhizopus, Agaricus mushroom, yeast) card sort into the five kingdom envelopes

quiz.prompt: Which of these is the correct way to write the binomial name of maize?
choices: Zea Mays
zea Mays
zea mays
Zea mays
quiz.rationale: In binomial nomenclature the genus name starts with a capital letter and the species name is entirely in lowercase. The name is italicised, or underlined when handwritten.
quiz.placement: Hierarchy card arrangement for maize: writing the binomial name Zea mays correctly

quiz.prompt: Which list shows the taxonomic ranks in the correct order, from the largest group to the smallest group?
choices: Kingdom, Class, Phylum, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Phylum, Order, Class, Family, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Genus, Family, Species
quiz.rationale: The correct hierarchy is Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. Each rank is nested inside the one before it.
quiz.placement: Hierarchy card arrangement (Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species) for maize

quiz.prompt: A learner says, "Spirogyra is an animal because it lives in water." Which response is the best scientific reply?
choices: Correct, because all organisms in water are animals.
Correct, because Spirogyra is too small to be a plant.
Wrong, because anything green must be a plant.
Habitat is not a reliable rule. We should use observable features such as cell type, chlorophyll and mode of nutrition.
quiz.rationale: Classification into kingdoms depends on shared observable features such as cell type, nutrition and chlorophyll, not on where an organism lives. This is why habitat-based sorting from Lesson 1 was not enough.
quiz.placement: Class discussion and debate: 'Is algae (Spirogyra) a plant?' using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning

quiz.prompt: Maize is called mahindi in Kiswahili, bhutta in some communities and corn in English. Why do scientists also give it one scientific name, Zea mays?
choices: One two-part name can be understood by scientists everywhere, whatever the local name.
Local names are wrong and must be replaced.
The scientific name tells where the plant grows.
Scientific names are always shorter than local names.
quiz.rationale: Binomial nomenclature gives each organism one universal two-part name. This lets people who use different local names communicate about the same organism.
quiz.placement: Connecting classification, nomenclature and taxonomy: 'Why did we need one scientific name when mahindi, bhutta and corn already exist?'

quiz.prompt: Why is correct identification and naming of organisms important for conserving biodiversity in forests such as Kakamega Forest?
choices: It stops species from changing over time.
It lets scientists know which species are present and which are rare, so they can protect them.
It makes all species belong to the same kingdom.
It means only the species useful to people need to be protected.
quiz.rationale: Taxonomy identifies and names species so that scientists can record them, find out which are rare or threatened, and plan protection. Conservation does not depend only on how useful a species is.
quiz.placement: Discussion of the importance of taxonomy: conserving biodiversity such as Mau Forest, Kakamega Forest and Mt Kenya

quiz.prompt: Which statement best describes taxonomy?
choices: Giving organisms local names in different languages
Grouping organisms only by where they live
The science of classifying, naming and identifying living organisms
The study of how organisms interact with their environment
quiz.rationale: Taxonomy is the science that groups organisms (classification), gives them universal two-part names (nomenclature) and helps identify them using observable characteristics.
quiz.placement: Final Explanation: 'How can living organisms be systematically organised, named and identified?' (Classification + Naming + Identification = Taxonomy)
